comment.value: In the revised paper, we have marked the major changes in blue, for the reviewer’s convenience in tracking them. We address to these changes in our responses to each reviewer below. Please kindly refer to the newest version of the paper when examining our responses.

title.value: Detailed clarification on the wide applicability of our proposed method.

comment.value:
**Weakness 1**

To clarify, we are stating that past observations
of pre-training and fine-tuning (PTFT) outperforming meta-learning are an artifact of
the benchmark tasks not being sufficiently diverse. Throughout our experiments, and
comparing to prior works using less diverse tasks, we find that pre-training and fine-tuning
(PTFT) performs worse, relatively speaking, as task diversity increases. DRESS can inject
sufficient task diversity into meta-training for it to perform well on diverse meta-testing
tasks.

To facilitate this discussion, we first needed to define and quantify task diversity. We noted
the deficiencies in prior work in **Section 2** (under the heading **Task Diversity**). Hence, we proposed
a more suitable metric and used it to quantify the diversity of various tasks in **Table 4**.
Whereas PTFT performs well on simple datasets used in prior work like miniImageNet and
CIFAR-FS, when we move to more diverse meta-testing tasks, the cracks in PTFT begin
to show, while DRESS continues to preform well (**Table 2**).
Of course, this does not rule out all possible other explanations and is not theoretical proof,
but it suggests that prior work on PTFT did not test on adequately diverse meta-testing
tasks, leading to hasty conclusions.

**Weakness 2** 

We agree with this comment. In **Section 1** we discussed past work
that observed exactly this—on low diversity datasets PTFT does well. However, our main objective was to point out that this trend does not continue for datasets with more diverse
tasks in the general problem of few-shot learning. Similarly, as the reviewer mentioned,
when the pre-trained encoder in PTFT has limited capacity, the resultant performance is
likely to degrade significantly.

**Weakness 3**

It is not the case that DRESS only works on medium diversity settings.
Low diversity settings, as studied in previous work (**Section 1**), can be solved with simple
approaches like PTFT, as well as meta-learning methods including DRESS. The gap in prior work is that high diversity settings
were not tested, and we have found PTFT insufficient here, while DRESS performs much
better (See **Table 1** and **2**). In our experiments, we did not observe an upper limit of
task diversity that DRESS can handle. Both the fundamental principle and the design of
DRESS are general and are not built on any assumption about the dataset complexity or
task diversity.

We emphasized the importance of high task diversity in the paper to address the confusing
findings in the literature where PTFT outperforms meta-learning algorithms. We deliberately chose datasets and formulated the task setups to cover a wide spectrum of task
complexities and diversities from low to high. Furthermore, we covered the out-of-domain
adaptation scenario with experiments on LFWA (**Table 2**). DRESS remains competitive
throughout these experiments.

Therefore, we kindly ask the reviewer to help clarify what evidence they saw in our work
that suggests the task diversity cannot be too high for DRESS.

U7QL: (1) lack of theoretical or empirical validation on the main claim about the limitation of current meta-learning methods. (2) Overlooking certain settings. (3) the proposed DRESS seem to work on certain task diversity and backbone network complexity.

jfVw: (1) the assumption of well-disentangled latent factors is not well examined. (2) limited novelty. (3) the "task diversity metric" is ad-hoc 

mUUa: (1) limited novelty/originality (2) the problem in the paper is addressed by recent advancement of foundation models.

The reviews of this paper are mixed. Reviewers generally agree with the motivation (task diversity for meta learning), they also expressed certain important concerns. In particular, AC finds the following concerns are important and not well addressed in the rebuttal. First of all, the novelty of the work is limited. It is well known fact that disentangled representation and task diversity are useful.  The proposed method essentially uses more advanced feature encoders to produce better (i.e. disentangled) representation, then use standard meta learning approach. The AC finds this novelty is incremental. Second, the AC finds that the concern mentioned by reviewer JfVw to be important. The datasets used in the paper are chosen to have certain factors of variations, while the encoders used in the proposed method are also precisely designed to handle certain disentangled factors. In some sense, the encoders are chosen to fit the datasets. It is important to evaluate whether the conclusions of the paper still hold when using other stronger pretrained backbone (e.g. DINOv2). Given these concerns, this paper is not ready for ICLR in its current form. Authors are encouraged to revise the paper and take into account of reviewers' comments for resubmission

title.value: Summary of Our Improvements and Responses

summary.value:
This paper proposes DRESS, a self-supervised meta-learning framework that constructs diverse few-shot tasks using disentangled representations.
The method trains an encoder (e.g., FDAE or LSD) to separate latent factors, aligns latent dimensions, clusters each dimension to form pseudo-classes, and uses them to meta-train a model with MAML.
Experiments on curated and real-world datasets show DRESS outperforming existing self-supervised and unsupervised meta-learning baselines, especially when task diversity is high.

strengths.value:
(1) The paper clearly motivates the link between task diversity and the failure of standard meta-learning benchmarks.

(2) The framework is conceptually interesting which using disentanglement to create pseudo-tasks is an intuitive way to increase diversity.

(3) The experiments are relatively broad, covering both synthetic datasets (Shapes3D, MPI3D, etc.) and realistic ones (CelebA, LFWA).

weaknesses.value:
(1) The entire approach hinges on having well-disentangled latent factors, but disentanglement models rarely achieve clean factor separation in practice; this assumption is barely examined.

(2) The claimed novelty over prior unsupervised meta-learning methods (e.g., CACTUS, Meta-GMVAE) is incremental. It replaces clustering in feature space with clustering along latent dimensions but doesn’t bring a real theoretical or algorithmic advance.

(3) The so-called “task diversity metric” is ad-hoc and does not correlate with adaptation performance; it’s unclear whether higher diversity actually improves meta-generalization beyond synthetic datasets.

questions.value:
(1) How robust is DRESS when the disentanglement isn’t perfect? In practice, disentangled features are often noisy or overlapping — does the whole task construction pipeline break down when that happens?

(2) How much does the method rely on the specific encoder choice (FDAE vs. LSD)? If we just use a strong pretrained backbone like DINOv2 without explicit disentanglement, does DRESS still work or does the advantage disappear?

(3) The paper claims that supervised labels can “misguide adaptation,” but that point feels hand-wavy. Can the authors actually show a concrete example or quantitative result where this happens?

(4) Why only test MAML? Would something simpler like ProtoNet or RelationNet also benefit from the proposed task construction, or is DRESS inherently tied to gradient-based adaptation methods?

summary.value:
This paper has a clear motivation or assumption that current few-shot learning benchmarks lack task diversity, which makes simple pre-training and fine-tuning approaches appear superior to meta-learning. This paper introduces DRESS (Disentangled REpresentation-based Self-Supervised meta-learning), a novel framework for few-shot learning that integrates disentangled representation learning with self-supervised meta-learning. 

To address this, DRESS constructs diverse self-supervised tasks and aligns latent dimensions to ensure semantic consistency,  then it clusters each latent dimension independently to form pseudo-classes, and creates varied few-shot tasks for meta-training using these clusters.

Comprehensive experiments on multiple datasets: SmallNORB, Shapes3D, Causal3D, MPI3D, CelebA, and LFWA, demonstrate that DRESS outperforms other baselines.

strengths.value:
1. The motivation is clear and strong.
2. The presentation is very well and the arguments are coherent.
3. Comprehensive experiments and ablation studies are conducted to validate the proposed approach.

weaknesses.value:
1. Disentangled encoder dependency: DRESS relies on disentangled representation models such as FDAE or LSD, which require substantial training resources and careful hyperparameter tuning. There are two concerns for this:
 - 1.1: The paper could discuss the computational trade-offs more explicitly.
 - 1.2: From the paper, "*all images available for meta-training are collected, and used to train a general purpose encoder*", it's confusing whether the pretrained model is also trained in this way or not. The difference should be clarified because the paper claims that in the scenario of task diversity scenario, meta-learning could outperform pretrained models. It seems meta-learning also has a pretrained encoder condition.

2. The task diversity metric validation is not enough: While intuitive, the proposed class-partition IoU metric’s correlation with downstream adaptation performance could be analyzed more deeply (e.g., correlation plots or regression). Could the proposed task diversity metric be integrated into the training process to encourage the model to sample or emphasize more diverse pseudo-tasks dynamically?

questions.value:
In addition to the questions in weakness, some additional questions:

1. It is reasonable that on simpler datasets such as Omniglot, where tasks are highly similar, meta-learning methods often underperform compared to pre-trained models. When constructing tasks with high diversity, could incorporating out-of-domain tasks be beneficial? Specifically, how does DRESS perform if the disentanglement model is pre-trained on a dataset different from the meta-learning dataset (i.e., under out-of-domain disentanglement)?

2. What is the computational cost of DRESS compared to baselines (such as CACTUS or Meta-GMVAE, etc.), for instance, in terms of GPU hours or memory usage?

title.value: Illustration on practical disentangled factors which support DRESS's performances,  further correlation analysis on the task diversity metric, and clarifications on the novelty and robustness of DRESS.

comment.value:
**Weakness 1**

We agree that well-disentangled latent factors are indeed hard to obtain.
However, this did not limit the practicality of DRESS which showed consistently strong
performance utilizing latent factors obtained on various image datasets. We only
use the concept of well-defined disentangled latent factors to motivate DRESS,
and proceed to show through experiments that this intuition holds up in practical settings. We examined the effect of non-ideal latent factors, particularly in the results under CelebA-Primary and CelebA-Random setups, under **Section 5.2**. In our ablations (**Table 3**) we also looked at the impact of using non-disentangled encoders.

In our revised paper we have included visualizations and
discussions on the latent factors that are actually learned. See the new **Appendix H**. Each latent factor is visualized
by its corresponding attention mask. As shown, while the learned disentangled factors correspond to different visual concepts within an image, they are not perfect due to the limitation from noise within the image and the
capacity of the encoder. Nonetheless, these factors are sufficient to support DRESS to
achieve the competitive performance reported in the paper.

**Weakness 2**

Our goal in this paper is to explore a roadmap that is broader than
proposing a single method. Firstly, a line of recent research identifies a confusing phenomenon that PTFT beats meta-learning
algorithms using much less information. We provide an explanation—
the lack of task diversity in evaluations, which we find to be a common issue in popular benchmarks. Therefore, we advocate for benchmarks incorporating more diversified tasks
requiring distinct logic to solve. Motivated by the importance of task diversity, we propose
DRESS, as the first method bridging meta-learning and disentangled representation learning, two fields which had not been studied jointly. Furthermore, to better quantify our idea, we propose a metric which, unlike the previous metrics in the
literature, is not bounded to any single embedding space.

**Weakness 3**

It is indeed worthwhile to analyze the correlation between our task
diversity metric and the adaptation performance. In our revised paper, in **Figure 5** under
**Section 5.4**, we include correlation plots on all datasets.
Especially for simpler datasets, the diversity of meta-training tasks is highly correlated
with the adaptation performance. On more complex datasets including CelebA, DRESS both creates the most diverse meta-training tasks, and achieves the best
performance compared to CACTUS-based methods.

**Question 1**

We hope our response to Weakness 1 addresses this question.

**Question 2**

In the original submission we had tested the DINOv2 backbone instead
of a disentangled encoder, see **Table 3** "DRESS w/o Disent. Repsent.". On most datasets there was a large drop in performance when using DINOv2 which suggests that disentangled latent features are genuinely
important to the method.

The choice of encoder is not as important. We used FDAE and LSD as two examples, but DRESS does not rely on their particulars.
As illustrated in **Appendix H** in our revised paper, these encoders produce disentangled
latent representations which are imperfect, yet DRESS manages to make good use of them.

**Question 3**

The Supervised-Original baseline exactly illustrates our claim that supervision can "misguide adaptation". As elaborated in **Section 4.4** and **Appendix B**, we reserve a subset of attributes from each dataset to create supervised
meta-training tasks for Supervised-Original, which is disjoint from the attributes used to
create meta-testing few-shot tasks. As shown in **Table 1** and **2**,
Supervised-Original performs poorly, and is surpassed by unsupervised baselines for
some setups. In **Section 5.1** and **5.2**, we discussed that when the supervised labels not match well with the meta-testing tasks, they can indeed misguide the model.

In our revised paper in **Section 4.3**, we added clarifications about the insights we can draw from each of the three supervised baselines.

**Question 4**

Regarding the compatibility of
DRESS, we have provided brief discussions in **Section 3.5** and more elaborations under **Appendix A**. To summarize, DRESS is not
inherently tied to gradient-based adaptation methods, but can benefit most meta-learning algorithms in general. As discussed under **Appendix A.2**, non-parametric
methods such as ProtoNet and RelationNet intrinsically assume one pre-defined latent
representation space, on top of which the classification is achieved. This design limits the ability for the model to generalize to tasks of different semantics. Therefore, although there is nothing technically prohibiting us from applying DRESS on Protonet or
RelationNet (or other Meta-learning algorithms for that matter), we have decided to use
MAML to best illustrate the capability of DRESS.

summary.value: To overcome the limitations of current meta-learning methods compared to pre-training and fine-tuning, the authors propose a simple addition to the few-shot learning task, where they add clustering-based disentangled representation learning for latent task embeddings to further diversify learning and aid generalization across tasks. They propose to generate self-supervised tasks by clustering along disentangled latent dimensions, thereby enforcing diversity among tasks. Experiments on controlled datasets (Shapes3D, SmallNORB, MPI3D, Causal3D) and real-world data (CelebA, LFWA) show that the proposed method achieves competitive results to existing meta-learning methods.

strengths.value:
- The perspective on fortifying the task diversity and its implementation through disentanglement and clustering-based approach seems straightforward and reasonable.

- The objective of the proposed method is explained in a straightforward manner, with simple formulation which can be easily implemented and reproduced by other researchers.

- The authors performed extensive experimental validations on multiple , and they also conducted some ablation experiments to facilitate further understanding for the proposed work.

weaknesses.value:
- Although the authors' main claim is that the limitations of current meta-learning methods come from the lack of task diversity in well-known meta-learning datasets such as miniImageNet and CIFAR-FS, it is not theoretically or empirically verified through thorough validation.

- Related to the previous question, the paper seems to conclude that it is better to use fine-tuning and pre-training approaches when there is a few-shot training dataset with small diversity. However, there are scenarios where the backbone feature extractor model lacks representational power (e.g. small in capacity), and this work seems to overlook this setting where conventional meta-learning can be dominant.

- Eventually, the proposed DRESS seems to only strike a middle ground where the task diversity is not too low, not too high, and the backbone network is not too simple, not too complex. This seems to limit the proposed work's wide application to various possible scenarios.

questions.value: Please refer to the weaknesses section. The insights found and the issues raised by the authors are still interesting and worth the analysis, but the applicability of the proposed method seems to be narrow, with limited usages.

summary.value: This paper introduces DRESS, a task-agnostic Disentangled Representation-based Self-Supervised meta-learning framework designed to enable rapid model adaptation across highly diverse few-shot learning tasks. Specifically, DRESS leverages disentangled representation learning to construct self-supervised tasks that enhance the meta-training process. The effectiveness of DRESS is demonstrated through experiments on datasets featuring multiple factors of variation and different levels of complexity.

strengths.value: This paper points out the limited task diversity in existing few-shot learning benchmarks, which explains why pre-training and fine-tuning sometimes appear to outperform meta-learning. To address this, the authors develop new few-shot learning benchmarks featuring more diverse tasks for rigorous evaluation. Furthermore, the paper introduces DRESS, a method that generates diverse tasks to enable self-supervised meta-learning through disentangled representations. Extensive experiments validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

weaknesses.value:
1.	First, meta-learning has been extensively explored over the past decades, and I believe it may no longer be a highly novel research direction.
2.	The disentanglement technique has been applied to many tasks, so I have concerns about the originality and novelty of this work.
3.	How many latent dimensions (“L”) are used in the model? As far as I know, increasing the number of latent variables will significantly enlarge the model size, which may not be an efficient strategy. Moreover, with the rapid advancement of foundation models that already exhibit strong generalization capabilities, I believe such models could potentially address the problems discussed in this paper.

questions.value: Please see the Weaknesses, I would like to see details of novelty.

title.value: Clarification on the novelty and potential of the work, further clarifications with details added in the revised paper.

comment.value:
**Weakness 1**

Our paper is not limited to proposing a specific meta-learning method,
but is focused on the grand picture of few-shot learning. We examined the reason why
meta-learning has seemingly been under-performing on few-shot learning tasks, namely the lack
of task diversity in the popular benchmarks. Correspondingly, we proposed DRESS,
and also formulated few-shot learning setups with tasks of distinct natures. Through these
results, not only do we showcase the effectiveness of our method, but we also illustrate
that meta-learning can still be the top choice when the problem setup truly incorporates
diversity. We hope our work can contribute towards reigniting the interest in meta-learning.

From another viewpoint, a major critique about many of the existing foundational models (especially
LLMs) is that they are merely mimicking human behavior. A popular idea within academia has been that we need
to revolutionize the way machines learn to actually achieve AGI. Meta-learning exactly
embodies the idea of learning-to-learn. Although there has not been recent meta-learning
research showing ground-breaking results comparable to the in-context learning abilities of LLMs for example, we still believe it is a direction with big potential. A great example is the DiscoRL work [1], which tackles Reinforcement Learning with machine-discovered rewards as inspired
by meta-learning. DiscoRL has been shown to achieve comparable or even better performance
than state-of-art RL algorithms with human designed update rules.

[1] Oh, Junhyk, et al. "Discovering state-of-the-art reinforcement learning algorithms." Nature. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41586-025-09761-x. 

**Weakness 2**

We agree that disentangled representations have been discussed in
many settings. However, it has been mostly investigated within the general
fields of representation learning and generative modelling. To the best of our knowledge,
our work is the first research to bridge the disentanglement representation learning with
meta-learning or few-shot learning, which have been two disjoint lines of research in the
literature.

**Weakness 3.1**

The choices of latent dimensions are discussed in **Section 3.1**. In our revised paper, we have included the number of attention slots (i.e.
the latent dimensions) in **Appendix D**, which ranges from 6 to 12.
In terms of the concern on the model capacity and computational efficiency, the number
of latent dimensions used by the encoder is not strictly tied with the capacity of the meta-learning model.
Therefore, the meta-learning model trained by DRESS can remain compact and light-
weight.

As for the encoders, the architectures we used (FDAE or LSD) have reasonable
sizes, comparable with all baselines. To better answer this concern, in the revised paper,
we have included the computation time required to train each encoder for each method in
**Appendix E**. As the matter of fact, the encoders we used are among the quickest to finish
training among baseline methods.

**Weakness 3.2**

We understand the reviewer’s concern, especially considering the recent
advance of foundational models, but did not find that recent foundation model encoders on their own address the problems we discussed. Firstly, foundational models come with much higher cost
from training data curation and computation required for training and inference. Further-
more, in the original paper we already tested a non-disentangled, but have strong, foundational model on vision tasks: DINOv2.  See **Table 3** "DRESS w/o Disent. Repsent." for an ablation where our disentangled encoder is swapped for DINOv2. Also, in
our baseline methods, CACTUS-DINO uses a standard few-shot learning approach with this strong foundational vision
encoder. As shown by the results, despite the high capacity and gener-
alization ability from DINOv2, DRESS is still able to provide better results for the majority
of the experiment setups. The results suggest that the benefit of learning from diversified
tasks constructed with explicit feature disentanglement can outweigh the capacity from a
foundational vision encoder.

Dear reviewers,

Sincere thanks to each of you for closely reviewing our paper. We hope our responses and modifications in the revised paper clarify your concerns and questions. If you have further question or would like more clarifications, we would be more than happy to follow up and discuss in details.

Thank you again for your consideration.

title.value: Additional analysis on computational complexity and the task diversity score, along with further clarifications.

comment.value:
**In the revised paper, we have marked the major changes in blue, for the reviewer’s convenience in tracking them.**

**Weakness 1.1**

For the encoders we utilized (i.e. FDAE
and LSD), both the model capacity and the number of hyper-parameters are comparable
with regular encoders. We found that disentangled encoders actually train slightly
faster than conventional encoders, likely due to their sparse connections among layers.
For concreteness, we measured the training time for each encoder on the complex CelebA dataset. The time for each method is as follows:

| LSD in DRESS        | DeepCluster in CACTUS | Meta-GMVAE | PsCo       |
|:-------------------|:--------------------|:-----------|:-----------|
| 8.5 hours           | 12.3 hours          | 7.0 hours  | 21.0 hours |


There is no major difference in the training required between DRESS and other methods. The
exception is DINOv2 used with CACTUS — DINOv2 was taken off-the-shelf, but took 3.3 days to train according
to the authors, presumably, on a large multi-GPU cluster. In the
revised paper, we have included this information as a table under **Appendix E**.
The numbers of hyper-parameters in the disentangled encoders are not substantially higher than that in conventional encoders used for baseline methods.
The most notable hyper-parameter that is unique to disentangled encoders is the number of disentangled latent dimensions, the selection of which is discussed in **Section 3.1**. Therefore, for the experiments we have conducted
throughout the paper, the process of hyper-parameter tuning for training disentangled encoders is not more costly than training regular encoders.

**Weakness 1.2**

We clarify that the same set of images is used for each of the following: 
1. training the encoder for obtaining embeddings used by meta-training tasks; 
2. performing meta-training; 
3. performing pre-training and fine-tuning (PTFT). 

The only exception is for experiments with DINOv2
which is of course pre-trained on a much larger set of data. Hence, our method DRESS
using disentangling encoders does not use an encoder that was pre-trained on additional
data compared to the PTFT baseline. In **Section 4.3** of the revised paper, we have added in
this clarification.

**Weakness 2**

In **Section 5.4** of our revised paper, we have expanded the discussion
of the task diversity metric. Specifically, we include a new correlation plot in **Figure
5** between the proposed task diversity score and the few-shot adaptation performance
during meta-testing. The results show strong correlations for simpler datasets including
SmallNORB, Shapes3D, and Causal3D, and relatively weaker yet still positive correlations
for complex datasets including MPI3D and CelebA.
For integrating the diversity score into the training process, we agree that this is a highly
promising direction for exploration. Possibilities include the use of active learning or curriculum learning during the meta-training stage. A comprehensive analysis is beyond the
scope of this review cycle. Thanks to this comment from the reviewer, we have noted this
as a potential direction in the revision paper under **Section 6**.

**Question 1**

Out-of-domain adaptation is indeed a natural experiment to examine and we covered it in our original submission in **Section 5.2**. Specifically, we used CelebA and LFWA for testing the out-of-domain few-shot adaptation capability of each method
which are more complex than Omniglot for example. Each method was meta-trained on
CelebA, then meta-tested on LFWA for few-shot adaptation. In **Table 2** we found that
DRESS still outperforms all the unsupervised baselines.

**Question 2**

For all the baselines, the computational cost is largely dominated by
the meta-training stage (few-shot adaptation during meta-testing is fast). In our revised
paper, we have included a table about the training duration under **Appendix E**. Training
the encoder is largely comparable between LSD for DRESS, DeepCluster for CACTUS,
and for Meta-GMVAE, on the order of 10 hours with a single GPU. For the meta-training stage after the tasks are constructed, each method takes around 3 hours.
